title: Against your will (Avot 4:22)
hookLine: against your will you were born, you live and you die, and still you give account
tomorrow: why would God need ten sayings to make one world?

cards: Every app makes you scroll the terms and tap agree. Life skipped that step. Nobody signed off on their birthday, their family, their hometown, the face in the mirror.

So if you were never asked, why would you still have to answer? Avot asks exactly that, in one strange breath. It says against your will, over and over, and then, in the same sentence, that you'll give account.

teach.b: Rabbi Elazar HaKappar closes chapter four with a heavy saying.

teach.h: AGAINST YOUR WILL, AGAIN AND AGAIN.
teach.b: Those born will die; the dead will live again; the living will be judged. Before God there's no wrong, no forgetting, no favoritism, no bribe. Don't let your inclination promise you the grave is a place to hide.
Then the refrain. Against your will you were formed. Against your will you were born.
Against your will you live. Against your will you die. And against your will you'll give account before the King of kings, the Holy One, blessed be He.
Here's the puzzle: if so much was never your choice, how is the account fair? Look at what's on the list. Being formed, being born, being alive, dying.
That's the frame, and nobody picks the frame.
What's not on the list is everything you did inside it. The account isn't for being born. It's for what you did with the life you were handed.
A midrash pictures the soul itself not wanting to go into the world, and sent anyway. The mishnah doesn't argue.
It just sets two things side by side: given, and still accountable. Some readers hear it as stern. Others hear fairness: an honest account, with nothing forgotten and nobody bought off.
You didn't choose the stage. The lines you say on it are yours.

how: In Jewish custom Pirkei Avot is read on summer Shabbat afternoons, a chapter a week; chapter four ends with Elazar HaKappar's saying, and the reader goes on to chapter five.

o: what happens to you without being asked
a vow you were pressured into keeping
a punishment for breaking God's law

games.q: the end of chapter four — tap the pairs.
p: for what you did with it

s: the mishnah says you're judged for being born
being born is on the list of what happens against your will. the account is for the life lived.
the same saying says no bribe works before God
no wrong, no forgetting, no favoritism, no bribe: the account is fair.

games.q: your coworker got moved to the night shift without being asked, and says, 'didn't choose it, so I'll just coast.' what would Elazar HaKappar point to?
o: the shift was handed to him; how he works it is still his to answer for.
coasting is fair: what's against your will isn't counted in the account.
he should fight the shift, since the account covers only what you choose.
games.why: the refrain lists what nobody chooses, then says you still give account. the frame is given; what you do inside it is yours.

practice: Rest your hands on your knees, palms up and open. One at a time, set into them the things you didn't choose: the family you were born into, the body you live in, the place you started. Don't argue with any of them.
For the last few breaths, let your fingers curl gently, the way you'd hold something handed to you.

wordCard.voice: Against your will: Elazar HaKappar's refrain for what nobody chooses. Being born, living, dying. And then, still, the account.

orig.note: Hebrew: against your will, the refrain of Avot 4:22.

carryVoice: Hold on to this one: given, and still accountable, the stage and then the lines. See you tomorrow.
